price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent H2-H1 change
regression to the mean in H1-to-H2 change
methodological_questions: Is a defense's opponent-adjusted H2-H1 effect stable across random game splits and across consecutive seasons?
Is the reliability distinguishable from zero given the small number of games per team-season and the noisy half-level efficiency?
How can the defense effect be separated from regression to the mean, opponent quality, score state, garbage time and rotation or minutes effects?
Is H2-H1 mechanically negatively correlated with H1 level, and does that create a floor or an artifact?

historical_evidence.finding: H1 play-type usage as a predictor of H2 suppression: matched ATT did not survive BH adjustment (PNR ATT +0.0313, BH_p 0.0658, WEAK; others NULL). Top-1 accuracy was 0.550 vs a mean-reversion baseline of 0.511 (+0.039). The record states the bulk of H2 suppression is RTM. n=8873 team-games.

Trigger attribution of H1->H2 PPP collapse: H1 PPP alone (RTM) explained 32.9% of variance and is 95% of the explained part. Usage, process, lineup and context added about 1.7 pp in total; 65.4% was unexplained and attributed to small per-half n. Recorded as a powered null (n=40963 cells).
Adapt vs continue matched-pair excess: the group B CI includes 0 (p=0.386, n=255). Group B is a reconstructed post-hoc cohort. Flagged PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE and SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER.

Inferred defensive scheme-change labels: 99% of units showed a change and the transition matrices were near-uniform. The record says this is consistent with label noise and cannot separate real defensive adjustment from the offense executing differently.
Descriptive shifts in play-type mix by half and context. The OTHER label is known to be noisy, and no inferential tests were run.
Descriptive team differences in how often H2 trigger possessions land on the BEST vs AVOID counter (team AVOID% 6.8% to 50.6%). No outcome test, and player samples were small (10-178 possessions).
Defensive play-type edges depend only on the defense (e.g. DAL PNR +9.2% against every offense) and are not matchup-specific. Descriptive only.
Equilibrium and actual-mix matchup predictors had negative R2 versus a team-mean R2 of +0.1197. Team-level means outperformed the more elaborate models. Recorded failure mechanism is a powered null.
Double-suppression stacking: the stacked effect was smaller than the additive prediction. Limited by small sample and an implementation bug.
Counter play-type specificity: median entropy 1.543, mostly matchup-specific. No inferential test.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Predicting H2 suppression from H1 usage, with matched ATT and a mean-reversion baseline
failed_approaches.why: Effects did not survive multiplicity correction and the lift over mean reversion was small (+0.039). Limited by selection or regression to the mean.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Explaining the variance of the H1->H2 PPP collapse with process, usage, lineup and context features
failed_approaches.why: RTM dominated the explained variance. The residual was idiosyncratic noise from small per-half n.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferring defensive scheme change from play-type labels
failed_approaches.why: Label or classification error; near-uniform transition matrices consistent with label noise.
Low power in the small group, a post-hoc cohort, and placebo dependence.

evidence_establishes: In the earlier play-type-level work, H1->H2 change is dominated by regression to the mean (FAM:SF-APPS-070, FAM:SF-APPS-076). A raw H2-H1 change is therefore not a defense trait without an H1 and opponent adjustment.
Per-half samples are noisy, and the earlier work attributes most residual variance to idiosyncratic noise (FAM:SF-APPS-076).
Inferred labels for defensive adjustment are unreliable (FAM:SF-APPA-005, FAM:SF-APPM-021).
Team-level static means were hard to beat in earlier prediction work (FAM:SF-APPA-020).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a team-level, opponent-adjusted H2-H1 defense effect has nonzero split-half or cross-season reliability. No retrieved record tests that estimand.
Whether any reliability exists for aggregate defense effects (points or PPP) as opposed to play-type suppression.
Whether the 120 team-seasons give enough power. No retrieved record reports the team-level reliability noise ceiling.
own_inferences: Per-game H2-H1 differences are noisy. With about 82 games per regular-season team-season, the sampling error of a team mean is probably the same size as or larger than any plausible true team SD, so reliability is likely low.

Opponent H2-H1 change is mechanically negatively related to opponent H1 level. A defense that is strong in H1 will look like it produces positive H2-H1 change, so an unadjusted trait could be an artifact of H1 defensive strength.
Part of any apparent trait could reflect the defense's own rotation or pace pattern and the schedule's opponent mix rather than a halftime counter-strategy effect.
The most likely competent outcome is a low-reliability null, or an uninterpretable result if the H1 adjustment is not done well. A modest positive result is possible but unlikely.
uncertainties: Whether 120 team-seasons means 30 teams x 4 seasons (regular season only) or includes playoffs, and whether 2025-26 is complete.
The true between-team SD of H2-H1 defensive effects is unknown, so power cannot be computed in advance.
Roster turnover between seasons limits the cross-season reliability ceiling even if a true trait exists.
Garbage-time and score-state handling is not described in the data description.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I might have proceeded with a plain split-half correlation of raw H2-H1 change. The retrieved records show that RTM dominates H1->H2 change and that per-half noise is large, so I moved to proceed_with_changes. The changes are an H1-adjusted residual outcome, opponent adjustment, a reliability noise ceiling and a permutation null. The records are about play-type suppression, so they do not decide the team-level question directly.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 120 team-seasons, and about 90 consecutive-season pairs; cross-season reliability will have a wide CI (r SE about 0.1) and a ceiling set by roster change.
H2-H1 is mechanically tied to the opponent's H1 level, so the outcome must be residualized on H1 and opponent expectation before any trait claim.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work found that H1->H2 suppression is mostly regression to the mean and that residual variance is mostly noise, but at the play-type level, not for a team defense's aggregate opponent H2-H1 effect. The team-level reliability question has not been directly tested in the retrieved records.

risks.text: Mechanical negative dependence between H1 level and H2-H1 change inflates or distorts any apparent defense effect, especially for teams selected as extreme.
Half-level efficiency per game is very noisy, so the reliability of the team mean is bounded by game-level noise.
120 team-seasons gives low power for cross-season stability; split-half uses within-season games but is limited by games per team.
Opponent offense quality, schedule, home/away, rest, score state and garbage time, starters' minutes and halftime lead all affect H2-H1 independently of the defense.
Roster, coaching and league-wide scoring or pace changes across 2022-26 reduce cross-season stability and shift the league-wide H2-H1 baseline.
Many outcome definitions (PPP, points, eFG, margin) and subgroups could be tried; only one primary outcome should count.

Using the same games to adjust the opponent baseline and to test reliability, or including playoff games from a later period, leaks information; adjustment should be fit out-of-sample or in a cross-fitted way.

design.estimand: Between-team variance share (reliability, ICC or split-half Spearman-Brown corrected correlation) of a defense's opponent-adjusted H2-H1 change: the opponent's H2 points per 100 possessions minus a prediction from that opponent's own H1 efficiency and season baseline, averaged over games. Secondary: the same quantity's correlation between consecutive seasons for the same franchise.
design.unit: Team-season (defense), with game as the repeated measure.
design.sample: Regular-season games from 2022-23 to 2025-26 (30 teams x 4 = 120 team-seasons; use 2025-26 only once complete, and exclude any partial data). Playoffs are a separate exploratory sample only. Exclude overtime periods and garbage-time possessions, defined by a prespecified margin and clock rule, from the primary analysis.
design.power: No power analysis is possible without the noise SD. The first step is to estimate the game-level SD of the adjusted outcome and the implied noise-only reliability ceiling from permutations. Treat as informative only if the 95% CI for reliability excludes both 0 and a smallest-interesting value (say 0.3). With about 90 consecutive pairs the SE of r is about 0.10, so a cross-season r below about 0.2 cannot be distinguished from zero; report as inconclusive in that case.
design.controls: Residualize each game's H2 efficiency on the opponent's H1 efficiency (fit league-wide, cross-fitted by season), the opponent's season offense rating, home/away, rest, pace, halftime margin and the defense's own H1 rating. Include opponent-offense fixed effects (mixed model with crossed random effects for defense and offense). Compare the defense random-effect variance with a model without it.
design.falsification: Permutation null: shuffle game-level adjusted outcomes within season across teams to get the noise-only reliability distribution. Placebo: apply the same procedure to Q1-vs-Q2 or an arbitrary odd/even half split, which should show no trait. Negative control: the offense's own H2-H1 trait should show reliability if the adjustment is working, and reliability of the defense effect should vanish after including the opponent's H1 level.
design.multiplicity: One primary outcome (opponent-adjusted H2 PPP residual) and one primary reliability statistic (split-half, 1000 random game splits). Cross-season stability, playoffs, other outcome definitions (eFG, margin) and subgroups are secondary and reported with BH correction.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if split-half reliability (Spearman-Brown) is at least 0.3 with a lower 95% bound above the permutation 95th percentile, and the cross-season correlation is positive with a CI excluding 0. Rejected if the upper CI of reliability is below 0.2 and the permutation test is not significant. Anything else is inconclusive, and an effect that disappears after H1-level adjustment is labelled an RTM artifact.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play, rotations and box-score files for NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26, as of 2026-10-06 (2025-26 regular season complete from 2026-04-13); freeze the data snapshot and the garbage-time rule before analysis.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent second-half adjustment
opponent H2-H1 change (second-half minus first-half scoring/efficiency)
methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change a stable team trait across seasons or split halves?
How many team-seasons are needed to detect a nonzero reliability given noise in half-level efficiency?
How to separate defense effect from regression to the mean, opponent quality, score-state and garbage-time confounding?
Is the H2-H1 outcome mechanically dependent on first-half performance, creating a mechanical floor or negative correlation?
args.query: defense effect on opponents' second-half minus first-half change as a reliable team trait; reliability, regression to the mean, 120 team-seasons

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 10 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.
